newsitem.title: USA: Hemophilia settlement garners 95 pct approval.
newsitem.headline: Hemophilia settlement garners 95 pct approval.

text.p: About 95 percent of the AIDS-infected hemophiliacs suing four drug makers have approved a $640 million settlement, the lead attorney for the class-action suit told a fairness hearing Monday in U.S. Federal Court in Chicago.

David Schrager said about 6,200 of the class members agreed to accept the settlement. Schrager told U.S. Senior District Judge John Grady about five percent of the other claimants have opted out to pursue independent litigation.
Schrager estimated there are about 800 other suits not part of the class action that still pending.
Judge Grady said he would take the matter under advisement and issue a ruling. He did not set a deadline for the ruling.
The judge already has given tentative approval to the agreement which would give each class member about $100,000.
The blood-clotting drugs were sold between 1979 and 1985 to hemophiliacs who later contracted AIDS.

They were manufactured by Germany's Bayer AG, Baxter International Inc, Armour Pharmaceuticals, a division of Rhone-Poulenc Rorer Inc and Alpha Therapeutic Corp, a division of Japan's Green Cross Corp.

In their suit, the hemophiliacs argued that the companies had failed to protect them from HIV by not heat treating the blood products and by taking blood products from people who were at high risk for contracting AIDS. The companies have said there were no reliable means for treatment of AIDS blood products until the mid-1980s.

In a separate joint statement, the four drug companies noted that the settlement is still conditioned on resolving reimbursement and subrogation issues, in which healthcare insurers may claim an interest in the settlement proceeds otherwise payable to affected members of the hemophilia community.
The companies said they will work with officials to resolve the reimbursement and subrogation matters to ensure that the settlement funds will go to those entitled to the proceeds.
